section_summary: This section contains monthly reports on internal conditions and foreign relations in Japan compiled by the American Embassy in Tokyo from January to June 1931 (with the May report missing and noted by an archival charge slip), alongside monthly transmission schedules of despatches and telegrams. The reports document major political developments including the contentious 59th Imperial Diet session, violent clashes between Minseito and Seiyukai factions, Baron Shidehara's acting premiership, and the resignation of Prime Minister Osachi Hamaguchi leading to the formation of the Wakatsuki Cabinet. External and colonial affairs featured prominently include the Russo-Japanese northern fisheries disputes, renewed uprisings in Formosa (Musha incidents), political unrest and administrative corruption scandals in Korea, Sino-Japanese tensions in Manchuria, royal ceremonies and state visits, and economic pressures stemming from the global depression.

subfiles.about: Embassy report transmitting the monthly political survey of internal, economic, and imperial conditions in Japan for January 1931, accompanied by lists of despatches and telegrams.
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires ad interim Eugene H. Dooman forwards Report No. 52 covering conditions in Japan during January 1931, including an index and complete lists of despatches and telegrams forwarded during the month. Major topics reviewed include the turbulent opening of the 59th Imperial Diet under acting premier Baron Shidehara due to Prime Minister Hamaguchi's continued incapacity, sharp public and Diet criticism of railway accidents on the Sanyo Line, the founding of the National Disarmament League, and the resignation of Governor-General Ishizuka following the Musha aboriginal revolt in Formosa. Further items cover the death of novelist Mrs. L. Adams Beck in Kyoto, the implementation of the Road Loan Law, acute unemployment among Tokyo university graduates contrasted with commercial bidding for star baseball players, the official rice crop count, preparations for the visit of the King and Queen of Siam, the decoration of General Chang Hsueh-liang in Mukden, and deadlocked freight negotiations between Japan and Soviet Russia in Manchuria.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 131: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan for January, 1931 (Report No. 52)

subfiles.about: Embassy report transmitting the monthly political survey of Japanese affairs for February 1931, detailing intense parliamentary discord, colonial unrest, and industrial labor issues, with lists of despatches and telegrams.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires ad interim Edwin L. Neville transmits Report No. 53 reviewing conditions in Japan for February 1931. The report highlights severe winter blizzards and an unprecedented political crisis in the Diet provoked by acting premier Baron Shidehara's slip of the tongue regarding the London Naval Treaty and the imperial prerogative, which led to a suspension of budget debate, a violent physical brawl between Minseito and Seiyukai supporters in Diet corridors, and protests by proletarian groups and the Women's League. In colonial and foreign affairs, it notes communist trials in Chientao, parliamentary controversy over the relocation of the South Chusei provincial office in Korea, the Tokyo District Court's acquittal of former Governor-General Hanzo Yamanashi on bribery charges, and a complete deadlock in Russo-Japanese fisheries negotiations over currency exchange rates. Domestic social matters include record high strike figures for 1930, nationwide shortfalls in municipal budgets for primary school teachers' salaries, and contentious debate over the revised government Labor Union Bill.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 160: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan for February, 1931 (Report No. 53)

subfiles.about: Embassy report transmitting the monthly survey of conditions in Japan for March 1931, reporting imperial family births, premier Hamaguchi's return to the Diet, and foreign negotiations, accompanied by lists of despatches and telegrams.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, Ambassador, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes submits Report No. 54 detailing events in Japan during March 1931, accompanied by lists of despatches and telegrams sent during the month. Significant domestic news includes the birth and christening of Princess Atsuko to the Empress, Prime Minister Hamaguchi's brief and physically frail appearance before the House of Representatives, intra-party discussions within the Minseito to choose his successor, the defeat of an opposition vote of non-confidence, street riots outside the Diet, and the defeat of the Woman's Civil Rights Bill in the House of Peers before the 59th session prorogued. External affairs covered include the attempted assassination of Soviet trade delegate Anikeeff by a Japanese malcontent named Sato, Sino-Japanese negotiations at Nanking regarding the abolition of extraterritoriality, the record-setting Paris-to-Tokyo flight of French aviators Burtin and Moench, and the voluntary renunciation of imperial status by Prince Kunihide Kuni after failing university entrance examinations.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 192: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan for March, 1931 (Report No. 54)

subfiles.about: Embassy report transmitting the monthly survey of Japanese political, colonial, and social conditions for April 1931, covering the resignation of Hamaguchi and formation of the Wakatsuki Cabinet, with lists of despatches and telegrams.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, Ambassador, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes transmits Report No. 55 summarizing events in Japan for April 1931 along with monthly lists of despatches and telegrams. The central political event was the long-expected resignation of Prime Minister Hamaguchi due to failing health following surgical operations, and the installation of Baron Reijiro Wakatsuki as Prime Minister and head of a reorganized Minseito Cabinet. In international and colonial developments, a temporary compromise on exchange rates was reached to settle the Russo-Japanese fisheries dispute, a second violent aboriginal uprising occurred in the Musha district of Formosa by the Tautsua clan against rival tribes, Chinese authorities imposed postal bans and communication restrictions on Japanese journalists in Nanking, and police arrested communist leader Yoshizo Iwata to halt the reorganization of the Japan Communist Party. The report also highlights the state visit of King Prajadhipok and Queen Rambhai Barni of Siam en route to America, the arrival of Edward Mooney as the first American Apostolic Delegate to Japan, and the severe economic crisis and declining numbers within the geisha profession caused by westernization and the depression.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 210: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan for April, 1931 (Report No. 55)

subfiles.about: Embassy report transmitting the monthly political survey of internal, colonial, and social developments in Japan for June 1931, accompanied by lists of despatches and telegrams.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, Ambassador, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes submits Report No. 57 covering Japanese affairs during June 1931, prefaced by comprehensive monthly schedules of despatches and telegrams sent to the Department. Key administrative reshuffles include the resignation of Admiral Viscount Makoto Saito as Governor-General of Chosen and the appointment of former War Minister General Kazunari Ugaki as his successor, alongside the resignation of Dr. Mitsugu Sengoku as president of the South Manchuria Railway and the appointment of Count Kosai Uchida to take charge of Manchurian railway policies and resolve disputes over Chinese parallel lines and Chinese export taxes on Fushun coal. Other sections cover the investigation into licensed prostitution quarters by the League of Nations Commission of Inquiry into Traffic in Women and Children led by Dr. Bascom Johnson, growing unemployment particularly among the westernized educated white-collar class ('yofuku-saumin'), Ministry of Education initiatives to revise school textbooks by reducing militaristic narratives, the return of Prince and Princess Takamatsu from their tour of Europe and America, and the first fatal commercial aviation disaster of the Japan Air Transport Company in Kyushu.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 261: Monthly Report on Conditions in Japan for June, 1931 (Report No. 57)
